# data/ — which file is which

There are now several label files with similar names, produced at different points and by
different people. This says which one is authoritative for what, because picking the wrong one
silently changes a number we quote on stage.

**When in doubt: `python doctor.py` from the repo root.**

---

## The reports (inputs — do not edit)

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `synthetic/synthetic_reports_for_labeling.csv` | 150 synthetic reports with site, activity, shift, report_date, is_contractor |
| `osha/osha_real_reports.csv` | 30 real OSHA Severe Injury Report narratives, ids 151–180 |

`report_id` is the join key everywhere. The OSHA file carries explicit `report_id` and `text`
columns — it used to carry only `report_text`, and three separate scripts reconstructed the ids
as `151 + row number`, so any re-export silently broke all three. **Do not remove those columns
or reorder the rows.**

OSHA rows have no site taxonomy, so they are excluded from every dashboard aggregate. That is a
stated limitation, not a gap to hide.

## Annotator files (one per person)

`gold_labels_<name>.csv` / `global_labels_<name>.csv` — 180 rows each, one annotator's own
judgements. Generated by `create_labeling_template.py`, filled by `label_reports.py` or by hand.

**These must never be edited after the two annotators have been compared.** The answer to *"you
wrote the reports and graded yourself"* is the published disagreement rate, not a ceiling: the
independent first round agreed 52.2%, kappa 0.083, which is why the severity gate was rewritten
instead of the labels quietly changed (see [../docs/hostile-qa.md](../docs/hostile-qa.md)). That
answer only holds if nothing was touched after the comparison.

Before handing one over:

```bash
python label_reports.py --annotator <name> --validate
```

That catches the failure that has already happened once here: `is_sif_precursor` typed by hand
instead of derived from the three gates. One annotator got it wrong on 138 of 180 rows, which
moved the headline agreement from a true 0.083 to a flattering 0.309.

## Derived files (regenerate, don't hand-edit)

| File | Produced by | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `gold_labels.csv` | `merge_labels.py` | rows both annotators agreed on — the training/eval set |
| `labeling_disagreements.csv` | `merge_labels.py` | rows needing M6's tiebreak |
| `disagreement_summary.csv` | ad-hoc | a narrower view of the same disagreements |

`gold_labels.csv` is what `train_baseline.py` and `eval/run_eval.py` read. It is incomplete until
M6's adjudicated rows are appended.

## Files with a history worth knowing

**`global_labels_sukanya2_corrected.csv`** — a post-hoc revision of that annotator's original.
It changed **163 of 180 rows**, including 74 flips of `is_sif_precursor`, and it was made after
the disagreements were visible. It raises measured agreement, which is what a revision made with
the disagreements in view would do.

**Do not use it to compute an agreement number anyone quotes.** It is fine as an input to
adjudication; it is not evidence about how well two people independently agree. No file in this
directory supports a ceiling claim — see the last section for the pass that would.

**`gold_labels_stub.csv`** — 15 rows of fake data from early scaffolding. Not real. Safe to
delete once nothing references it.

---

## The one check before quoting any number

```bash
python check_independence.py --a <A>.csv --b <B>.csv \
       --baseline-a <A_original>.csv --baseline-b <B_original>.csv
```

It reports whether each annotator derived the label or typed it, agreement computed both ways,
per-gate agreement, and how far each file drifted from its original. It deliberately does not
decide whether a revision was legitimate — only the team knows that — but it shows the
fingerprints, so the answer can be honest rather than hopeful.

A legitimate second round exists on paper: the rubric fails its check, gets revised (see the
changelog in [../docs/rubric.md](../docs/rubric.md)), and **both** annotators re-label from
scratch without conferring. That produces a real ceiling. Round two here did only the first half
— the annotators did not work independently the second time — and both rounds used rubric v2.1, so the revision
helped, not a ceiling. `prepare_independent_recheck.py` samples 40 reports for the independent
pass that would give us one; the worksheets are already at `recheck_akanksha.csv` and
`recheck_sukanya.csv`. Adjudicated files never produce a ceiling either — their agreement is
high by construction.
